newsitem.title: INDIA: India political crisis puts president in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: India political crisis puts president in spotlight.

text.p: President Shankar Dayal Sharma, usually little more than a figurehead, could point the way to settling India's political crisis now that Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government has fallen.
India's 47-year-old constitution bestows largely ceremonial duties on the president.
But in a crisis, the Cambridge-educated Sharma wields critical authority that allows him to decide which politician will form the government or to call elections.

Deve Gowda submitted the resignation of his 10-month-old centre-left government after being soundly defeated in a vote of confidence in parliament late on Friday. Sharma asked him to stay on as caretaker pending "alternative arrangements".
Sharma has indicated that he would prefer not to have to order the second general election in a year, and wants the political formations to try to cobble together a new majority.
Constitutional experts said that Sharma, a lawyer, would seek to satisfy himself that any candidate for the job of prime minister could guarantee a stable government.

"The president must now explore the possibility of bringing into existence a coalition that would allow the house of the people to serve out its full term," K.K. Venugopal, an eminent constitutional lawyer, told Reuters.
In May last year, Sharma turned to the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to form the government after a general election yielded a hung parliament.
The right-wing party is the largest single group in the 542-member lower house with 162 seats.

The BJP government held power for 12 days but resigned in the face of certain defeat ahead of the confidence vote. It was succeeded by the 15-party United Front coalition which was able to prove a majority, but only with Congress's backing.

The BJP has said it would stake a new claim to power only if it were able to muster a majority -- an unlikely prospect given the aversion in the United Front and Congress camps to allying with the Hindu nationalist party.
The Congress, which has 140 seats, does not relish the prospect of an early election but it lacks the needed votes.
Party chief Sitaram Kesri, who provoked the crisis by withdrawing Congress's make-or-break support to Deve Gowda's government, had earlier said he wanted to stake a claim to power.
But on Saturday, asked if he would ask the president for the right to forge a new majority, Kesri said: "That is not the most important issue."
The acrimony generated between the Congress and the United Front during the crisis may not be resolved quickly, even though both parties share the aim of frustrating the BJP bid for power.

"All these people will now have to work it out among themselves," a presidential aide told Reuters. "Only if they come out with communications to the president will he invite someone to attempt to form the government."
No group had yet staked a claim, he said.
If after a reasonable time Sharma were convinced no one could offer a stable government, he would consider dissolving the house and calling a general election, the aide said.
"Sharma would not possibly settle for a conglomeration of parties where he is not very certain that it would last out the full term," Venugopal said.
"So unless the leader of each political group is able to convince him that the coalition will stick together on policy and principle, he could call fresh elections."
